items.title: 20.2.1 Tools used in Recombinant DNA Technology

source_refs.note: Topic 20.2.1 as printed, with the For information box and Figures 20.1 and 20.2 at their printed places (PDF 156-157).

blocks.text: The gene of interest is the gene which is to be manipulated. The gene of interest can be obtained by one of the following three ways:

items: Direct synthesis of the gene of interest in the lab by using different enzymes (e.g., polymerases and ligases).
Synthesis by doing reverse transcription of its mRNA by using reverse transcriptase enzymes.
Cleavage from chromosome by using enzymes restriction endonucleases.

blocks.text: These enzymes cut specific sequences of nucleotides in DNA. They are also called molecular scissors. There are many kinds of restriction endonuclease. Each kind recognizes a specific nucleotide sequence in a DNA. Such a sequence of nucleotides is called restriction site or recognition region. The enzyme binds to the DNA at that sequence, and cuts the DNA at a particular place within this site.

blocks.alt: A long DNA duplex with two recognition sites, GAATTC on the top strand and CTTAAG on the bottom strand. Triangles mark the cut between G and A on each strand. A green arrow labelled 'Action of enzyme' leads to three fragments: the middle piece has single-stranded AATT overhangs at both ends, and the end pieces have matching overhangs.
blocks.caption: Figure 20.1: Action of restriction endonuclease (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 20.1).

blocks.title: For information
blocks.text: Restriction endonucleases are valuable due to the fact that any two DNA fragments produced by the same restriction endonuclease can be joined together.

The restriction sites have palindromic sequences of four to eight nucleotides. This means the nucleotides at one end of the restriction site are complementary to those at the other end. So, the two strands of the DNA have the same nucleotide sequence running in opposite directions at the restriction site. Restriction endonuclease binds to and cleaves both strands. After cleavage, both DNA fragments have single-stranded ends (a few nucleotides long) that are sticky i.e., complementary to each other.

Special molecules called vectors (or molecular carrier) are used for the introduction the of gene of interest into host cells. The gene of interest is attached to the vector and the vectors becomes a recombinant DNA (rDNA). Then, the rDNA is introduced into the host cells. The plasmids of bacteria are the most commonly used. Other vectors include;

items: Cosmids (plasmids that contain a small region of bacteriophage DNA called the cos sequence)
P1 artificial chromosomes (have features of both P1 vectors and Bacterial Artificial Chromosomes)

blocks.text: Animal viruses (e.g., human cold virus) also serve as vectors to carry genes of interest into monkey and human cells.

blocks.alt: Source DNA with the gene of interest (pink) between two cut sites is cut by a restriction endonuclease into pieces with stepped ends, releasing the gene of interest. A ring-shaped vector (plasmid) is cut by the same enzyme into a cleaved vector. The gene of interest goes into the cleaved vector, and the two join into a ring of recombinant DNA.
blocks.caption: Figure 20.2: Use of Vector (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 20.2).
blocks.long_description: Labels: Restriction endonuclease, Gene of interest, Vector (Plasmid), Cleaved Vector, Recombinant DNA.

blocks.text: This enzyme joins two DNA fragments. Therefore, it is called molecular glue. It forms the phosphodiester linkage between two adjacent nucleotides.

Expression system means a suitable organism that can act as host for rDNA (gene of interest attached with vector) and can express the gene of interest. The selection of suitable expression system depends upon the type of vector used to make rDNA. Bacterial cells act as an ideal expression system because of their short generation time and simple genetic system.
